title: visionOS: Windows, Volumes and Ornaments
theory: visionOS is the operating system of Apple Vision Pro and brings spatial computing: your app lives alongside the user's real surroundings. By default an app runs in the 'Shared Space', where windows and volumes from several apps coexist side by side; when it needs more, it opens a 'Full Space' with 'ImmersiveSpace', and then only your app is visible (in 'mixed', 'progressive' or 'full' styles). A regular window is a SwiftUI 'WindowGroup', just like on iOS, floating in space; for bounded 3D content you use a volumetric window with '.windowStyle(.volumetric)' and 'defaultSize(width:height:depth:in:)'. Ornaments (the '.ornament' modifier) are controls attached to the edge of a window, such as toolbars, that do not take space from the content. 3D content is built with 'RealityView' (which hosts RealityKit entities: 'Entity' + 'Component', such as 'ModelComponent' and 'CollisionComponent') or, more simply, with 'Model3D' to display a USDZ model. Input is by eyes and hands: the user looks at an element and pinches, which is equivalent to a tap; so targets must be large (at least about 60 pt) and 3D entities need 'InputTargetComponent' and 'CollisionComponent' to receive gestures such as '.gesture(TapGesture().targetedToAnyEntity())'. Think about comfort: do not lock content to the head, avoid abrupt motion and place windows at eye level. You test in the Apple Vision Pro simulator in Xcode, which simulates gaze and hands with the mouse, and you can reuse a lot of SwiftUI code from iOS and iPadOS. Common mistake: forgetting to declare the 'ImmersiveSpace' in the 'App' before calling 'openImmersiveSpace'.
corporateCase: A furniture decoration app for a retailer shows the catalog in a regular window and the chosen sofa in a volumetric window with 'Model3D', which the customer rotates by hand. The color and purchase buttons sit in an ornament under the window, without covering the product.
gameCase: A board game uses a volumetric window for the 3D board over the player's real table, with pieces as RealityKit entities that respond to gaze and pinch. For the special level, the game opens an 'ImmersiveSpace' that transports the player to a fantasy city.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Shared Space and Full Space in visionOS?
options: In the Shared Space the app takes over the whole environment; in a Full Space it shares the screen
Shared Space is only for games and Full Space only for productivity apps
In the Shared Space several apps coexist; in a Full Space only your app is shown
There is no difference; they are alternative names for the same mode
quiz.explanation: Every app starts in the Shared Space, coexisting with others. When it opens an 'ImmersiveSpace' it enters a Full Space, where only your content appears and the app gains access to more capabilities.

quiz.question: How does the user 'tap' a button in visionOS?
options: By looking at it and making a pinch gesture with the fingers
By physically touching a touch-sensitive screen with the hand
By pointing a controller with physical buttons
quiz.explanation: In visionOS selection is look + pinch, equivalent to the iOS tap. That is why 'Button' and 'TapGesture' work without changes.

quiz.question: What does the code '.windowStyle(.volumetric)' do?
options: It makes the window transparent and borderless
It opens a full-screen immersive space
It locks the window to the user's head
It creates a window with depth that shows bounded 3D content
quiz.explanation: A volumetric window is a 3D volume in the Shared Space. It is not immersive: other apps remain visible around it.

quiz.question: What are ornaments for?
options: To decorate the real environment with virtual objects
To attach controls to the edge of a window without using the content area
To open secondary windows of the app
quiz.explanation: Ornaments stay attached to the window (for example, below it) and are ideal for toolbars and buttons, keeping the main content free.

quiz.question: Which combination lets a RealityKit entity receive a tap gesture?
quiz.explanation: RealityKit uses the Entity-Component model. For the system to detect gaze/pinch, the entity must be an input target and have a collision shape. Without that the gesture never fires.

quiz.question: Which practice improves comfort in visionOS?
options: Putting small text very close to the eyes to save space
Moving the whole environment quickly for impact
Locking windows to the user's face so they follow it
Placing content at eye level and avoiding abrupt motion or head-locked items
quiz.explanation: Head-locked content and large, fast movements cause discomfort. Large targets, a comfortable distance and few sudden changes make use pleasant.

quiz.question: How do you test a visionOS app without a physical Apple Vision Pro?
options: By running in the Apple Vision Pro simulator in Xcode
By running the app directly on a connected iPhone
It is impossible to test without the device
By using only SwiftUI Previews on macOS
quiz.explanation: Xcode includes an Apple Vision Pro simulator in which mouse and keyboard simulate gaze and hands. For real sensors and performance, testing on the device is still recommended.

quiz.question: You have a SwiftUI iPad app and want to bring it to visionOS. What is the best approach?
options: Reuse the SwiftUI views and adapt windows, target sizes and, if it makes sense, add volumes and ornaments
It is impossible to reuse code between the platforms
quiz.explanation: SwiftUI is shared across Apple platforms. You add the visionOS destination and then enrich it with spatial features instead of starting from scratch.

extraQuiz.question: What is a 'Model3D'?
options: A component that applies physics to an entity
A SwiftUI view that displays a 3D model (such as a USDZ) simply
extraQuiz.explanation: 'Model3D' loads the model asynchronously and shows it like a regular view. For more complex interaction use 'RealityView' and entities.

extraQuiz.question: You called 'openImmersiveSpace(id: "cena")' and nothing opened. What is the most likely cause?
options: The simulator does not support SwiftUI
The 'ImmersiveSpace(id: "cena")' was not declared in the 'App'
The main window must be volumetric
extraQuiz.explanation: The immersive space is a scene and must be declared in the 'body' of the 'App' with the same 'id'. Only then can the environment action open it.

extraQuiz.question: What are 'Component's in RealityKit?
options: Pieces of data and behavior attached to an 'Entity'
extraQuiz.explanation: RealityKit follows the Entity-Component pattern: the entity is a container, and components such as 'ModelComponent' or 'CollisionComponent' define what it is and does.

extraQuiz.question: What is an appropriate interactive target size for look + pinch?
extraQuiz.explanation: Since gaze is less precise than a finger on a screen, targets must be generous. Small, tightly packed controls make selection hard.

extraQuiz.question: Which immersion style lets the user see the real world mixed with the app's content?
options: None: visionOS never shows the real world
extraQuiz.explanation: 'mixed' blends virtual content with the real environment; 'full' replaces everything with a virtual environment and 'progressive' lets the user adjust the amount with the Digital Crown.

extraQuiz.question: What is the main difference between a regular window and a volumetric one?
options: The volumetric one has depth and holds 3D content, while the regular one is a 2D surface
The regular one is immersive and the volumetric one is not
The volumetric one only works in a Full Space
extraQuiz.explanation: Both live in the Shared Space. The regular one shows 2D interface (with merely decorative depth); the volumetric one defines a volume for 3D objects the user can walk around.

title: watchOS: Interface, Complications and Workouts
theory: Apple Watch is used in glances of a few seconds, so design must prioritize essential information, short text, large controls and flows with few taps. On watchOS, SwiftUI is the foundation: 'NavigationStack' organizes stack navigation, 'TabView' with '.tabViewStyle(.page)' creates swipeable pages and the '.digitalCrownRotation($value)' modifier binds the Digital Crown to a value. Complications and Smart Stack widgets are built with WidgetKit, using families such as 'accessoryCircular', 'accessoryRectangular', 'accessoryInline' and 'accessoryCorner' and a timeline of entries that the system displays without opening the app. Workouts use HealthKit: you set up an 'HKWorkoutConfiguration', create an 'HKWorkoutSession' with the 'HKHealthStore' and an 'HKLiveWorkoutBuilder' to collect heart rate and calories; during an active session the app keeps running in the background, which requires the HealthKit capability and the workout background mode. Outside workouts, background execution is limited: the system grants refresh tasks with a tight budget, so the app should update data sparingly and reload timelines only when needed. An app can be independent (works without the iPhone, with its own networking) or a companion; when both sides talk, you use the WatchConnectivity 'WCSession' ('updateApplicationContext', 'transferUserInfo' and 'sendMessage', the latter only when the other side is reachable). Haptics via 'WKInterfaceDevice.current().play(_:)' give discreet feedback but should not be overused. Battery is a scarce resource: avoid continuous animations, polling and unnecessary work.
corporateCase: A gym chain's app offers the day's workouts on the watch in a 'NavigationStack' and a complication showing the next scheduled class. The app is independent, so members can log a workout even when they leave the iPhone in the locker.
gameCase: A pocket racing game uses the Digital Crown to control the character's speed and haptics to signal a completed lap. A complication on the watch face shows the player's current record, updated by a WidgetKit timeline.

exercises.question: Access the shared WatchConnectivity session
exercises.hint: It is the static property that returns the single instance, written with the English word for 'standard'.

quiz.question: Which design principle is most important on Apple Watch?
options: Put as much information as possible on the screen
Replicate the entire interface of the iPhone app
Show the essential information quickly, with few interactions
Require long sequences of taps to finish a task
quiz.explanation: The watch is checked in glances. Lean screens, short text and large targets work better than dense interfaces.

quiz.question: What does '.tabViewStyle(.page)' do on watchOS?
options: It turns the TabView into pages the user swipes through
It creates a fixed bottom tab bar
quiz.explanation: With the '.page' style, each child of the TabView becomes a page and the user switches between them by swiping, with page indicators.

quiz.question: How are complications/widgets built on current watchOS?
options: With a loop that updates the watch every second
With WidgetKit, describing a timeline of entries
quiz.explanation: WidgetKit lets the system display timeline entries without opening the app. You choose families such as 'accessoryCircular' and 'accessoryRectangular' for each kind of space.

quiz.question: What is needed to collect data during a workout on the watch?
options: An 'HKWorkoutSession' with HealthKit authorized and the matching capability
quiz.explanation: The HealthKit workout session keeps the app active and collecting data, such as heart rate, even with the wrist lowered. The user must authorize reading the data types.

quiz.question: Which statement about background execution on watchOS is true?
options: Any app can run in the background indefinitely
Outside a workout session, background run time is limited and controlled by the system
The app never receives refresh tasks
Background time is unlimited if the watch is charging
quiz.explanation: The system grants background tasks with a tight budget to preserve battery. Active workout sessions are the exception, since the user is actively exercising.

quiz.question: When does WCSession's 'sendMessage' work?
options: Always, even with the other app closed and the device off
Only when the iPhone is unlocked and on Wi-Fi
When the other side is reachable at that moment
quiz.explanation: 'sendMessage' is for immediate communication and requires 'isReachable'. For data that can wait, 'updateApplicationContext' and 'transferUserInfo' deliver later.

quiz.question: What characterizes an independent watchOS app?
options: It works without requiring a companion app installed on the iPhone
It only runs with the iPhone nearby
quiz.explanation: An independent app is installed and used directly on the watch, using the Apple Watch's own networking, and can still sync with the iPhone when that adds value.

quiz.question: Which practice helps save battery on watchOS?
options: Updating the interface 60 times per second
Keeping a network connection open all the time
Avoiding continuous animations and polling, updating data only when needed
quiz.explanation: Every update consumes energy, and calls to reload timelines have a limited budget. Updating on demand and using notifications or background tasks is the way.

extraQuiz.question: Which widget family is circular for the watch face?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'accessoryCircular' is a round complication; 'accessoryInline' is a line of text and 'accessoryRectangular' is a rectangle. The 'system' families are for iPhone and iPad.

extraQuiz.question: What is 'HKLiveWorkoutBuilder' for?
options: Collecting and organizing data in real time during a workout
extraQuiz.explanation: The builder, associated with an 'HKWorkoutSession', receives samples such as heart rate and active energy and, at the end, saves the workout to HealthKit.

extraQuiz.question: Which WatchConnectivity method suits syncing the latest settings state without requiring immediate delivery?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'updateApplicationContext' sends the most recent context; if there are several sends, only the last one matters. It is ideal for settings and current state.

extraQuiz.question: What can the Digital Crown do in a SwiftUI app?
options: Replace the need for any touch
Provide precise rotation input bound to a value
extraQuiz.explanation: With '.digitalCrownRotation', rotation updates a variable, useful for scrolling lists or adjusting values precisely.

extraQuiz.question: What is a good use of haptics?
options: Vibrating continuously while the app is open
Vibrating every second like a clock
Discreetly confirming an important action, such as the end of an exercise set
extraQuiz.explanation: Haptics should be occasional and meaningful. Excessive use annoys the user and drains the battery.

extraQuiz.question: In a WidgetKit timeline, what does each entry represent?
options: The content the complication will show at a point in time
extraQuiz.explanation: The timeline is a list of dated entries. The system presents them at the right time, without needing to run the whole app all the time.

title: macOS: Windows, Menus and Document-Based Apps
theory: Mac apps have their own conventions: several windows, a menu bar, keyboard shortcuts, a sidebar and files. In SwiftUI, an 'App' declares scenes: 'WindowGroup' creates windows that can have multiple instances, 'Window' represents a single window with an identifier, and 'Settings' defines the preferences window opened automatically by Cmd+,. Menus are customized with the '.commands { }' modifier, where 'CommandMenu("Title")' adds a whole menu and '.keyboardShortcut("n", modifiers: .command)' binds shortcuts to buttons. The toolbar uses '.toolbar' with 'ToolbarItem', and typical three-column navigation uses 'NavigationSplitView' with sidebar, list and detail. Document-based apps use 'DocumentGroup' with a type that adopts 'FileDocument' (or 'ReferenceFileDocument'): you implement 'readableContentTypes', 'init(configuration:)' and 'fileWrapper(configuration:)', and the system provides open, save, undo and version history. The App Sandbox isolates the app and each access (user-selected files, network, camera) requires an entitlement, such as 'com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write' and 'com.apple.security.network.client'. 'MenuBarExtra' creates an item in the menu bar, useful for utilities, and 'NSViewRepresentable' (with 'makeNSView' and 'updateNSView') lets you embed AppKit views in SwiftUI. For distribution, the Mac App Store requires the sandbox; outside it you use Developer ID with Apple notarization and the hardened runtime, so that Gatekeeper accepts the app.
corporateCase: An accounting firm builds a Mac app to edit reports in its own format, with 'DocumentGroup', keyboard shortcuts and a sidebar listing the sections. Because the app is distributed outside the Mac App Store, it is signed with Developer ID and notarized before being delivered to clients.
gameCase: An indie studio makes a level editor for its Mac game, where each level is a document saved to disk, with a custom 'Ferramentas' menu and shortcuts for each brush. A 'MenuBarExtra' shows the level build status while the editor is in the background.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'WindowGroup' and 'Window' on macOS?
options: 'Window' allows multiple instances and 'WindowGroup' only one
Both always create exactly one window
'WindowGroup' allows multiple window instances; 'Window' is a single window
quiz.explanation: 'WindowGroup' is the default choice (Cmd+N opens new windows). 'Window' is useful for a single window, such as a log panel or a utility window.

quiz.question: How do you add a complete menu to the app's menu bar?
quiz.explanation: The '.commands' modifier customizes the menu bar. 'CommandMenu' creates a new menu, and 'CommandGroup' lets you change existing menus.

quiz.question: What must a type do to be used in a 'DocumentGroup'?
options: Adopt 'FileDocument' (or 'ReferenceFileDocument') and declare the supported content types
quiz.explanation: The system calls 'init(configuration:)' to read and 'fileWrapper(configuration:)' to write. 'readableContentTypes' says which files the app opens.

quiz.question: In the App Sandbox, what is needed for the app to read a file the user chose in an open panel?
options: No entitlement, the sandbox allows everything
quiz.explanation: The sandbox blocks by default. With 'com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-only' (or read-write) the app accesses exactly the files the user chose.

quiz.question: Your sandboxed Mac app makes HTTPS calls to an API, but they all fail. What is the likely cause?
options: The outgoing network client entitlement is missing
The app needs to be notarized
quiz.explanation: With the sandbox enabled, outgoing connections require 'com.apple.security.network.client'. Without it the system blocks the network, even if the code is correct.

quiz.question: What is 'NSViewRepresentable' for?
options: To use a SwiftUI view in UIKit
To create a menu bar item
To use an AppKit view inside a SwiftUI hierarchy
quiz.explanation: You implement 'makeNSView(context:)' to create the view and 'updateNSView(_:context:)' to sync it with SwiftUI state, useful when AppKit has features SwiftUI does not yet have.

quiz.question: What is the distribution difference between the Mac App Store and Developer ID?
options: On the Mac App Store the sandbox is mandatory; with Developer ID it is not, but the app must be signed and notarized
Developer ID requires the sandbox and the Mac App Store does not
Notarization only applies to the Mac App Store
quiz.explanation: Outside the store you distribute the app yourself (from a website, for example), but Apple's notarization and the hardened runtime make Gatekeeper accept it without scary warnings.

quiz.question: Which SwiftUI modifier adds buttons to the window's toolbar?
quiz.explanation: '.toolbar' declares the window's toolbar items. Each 'ToolbarItem' can have placement, such as primary or navigation.

extraQuiz.question: Which scene should you use to show an icon in the menu bar?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'MenuBarExtra' creates a menu item with an icon and content. With the '.window' style it shows a full SwiftUI view instead of a simple menu.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'Settings' do automatically?
options: It connects the preferences window to the app menu's 'Settings' item and to the Cmd+, shortcut
It opens the app in full screen
extraQuiz.explanation: SwiftUI integrates the 'Settings' scene with the app menu, so you only describe the content.

extraQuiz.question: What is the role of the 'hardened runtime' in distribution outside the store?
options: It is a security requirement for notarization
It replaces the sandbox for the Mac App Store
It is only used in iOS apps
extraQuiz.explanation: Notarization requires Developer ID signing and the hardened runtime enabled. Apple scans the app and returns a ticket that Gatekeeper recognizes.

extraQuiz.question: Which view is the basis for a three-column interface with a sidebar?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'NavigationSplitView' manages sidebar, content column and detail, adapting to the window size.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'keyboardShortcut("s", modifiers: .command)' do?
options: It automatically saves the file in every case
It binds Cmd+S to the button or menu item
extraQuiz.explanation: The shortcut only triggers the action of the control it was applied to. Actually saving depends on the action's implementation.

extraQuiz.question: Your menu bar app should not appear in the Dock. Which approach exists?
options: Configure the app as an agent (LSUIElement) in Info.plist
extraQuiz.explanation: The 'LSUIElement' key (Application is agent) makes the app show no Dock icon or main menu, which is common in menu bar utilities.

title: Games with SpriteKit and GameKit
theory: SpriteKit is Apple's 2D framework for games and animations. An 'SKView' presents an 'SKScene', which is the root of a tree of 'SKNode's; visible nodes include 'SKSpriteNode' (images), 'SKLabelNode' (text) and 'SKShapeNode'. The scene's origin is at the bottom-left corner and the y axis grows upward. Animations use 'SKAction' ('move(by:duration:)', 'fadeOut', 'sequence', 'repeatForever') run with 'node.run(_:)'. The game loop runs every frame: the system calls 'update(_:)' on the scene, evaluates the actions and simulates physics, and you put the continuous logic there, using the received time to compute deltas. Physics bodies ('SKPhysicsBody') have 'categoryBitMask', 'collisionBitMask' and 'contactTestBitMask'; to be notified of a contact, 'physicsWorld.contactDelegate' must be set and 'didBegin(_:)' receives an 'SKPhysicsContact'. In SwiftUI, 'SpriteView(scene:)' hosts a scene, which must be created once (for example, in a property) and not inside 'body'. Touches arrive through 'touchesBegan' on the scene or on nodes with 'isUserInteractionEnabled'. GameKit adds Game Center: you authenticate the player with 'GKLocalPlayer.local.authenticateHandler', submit scores to leaderboards and report achievements, all configured in App Store Connect. For performance, reduce the node count, remove nodes that left the screen with 'removeFromParent()', use texture atlases ('SKTextureAtlas') and watch 'showsNodeCount' and 'showsFPS' during development.
corporateCase: An education company builds a math game for children with SpriteKit hosted in a 'SpriteView' inside a SwiftUI app. Game Center leaderboards motivate classes to compete in a healthy way, and the game keeps 60 frames per second by reusing textures from an atlas.
gameCase: In a spaceship game, 'update(_:)' moves the background and spawns enemies; ships and bullets have different bit mask categories, and 'didBegin(_:)' detects the collision to remove the enemy and add points. At the end of the match the score is submitted to the Game Center leaderboard and an achievement unlocks after defeating 100 enemies.

quiz.question: What is the origin of an SKScene's default coordinate system?
options: Top-left corner, with the y axis growing downward
Always the center of the screen, without exception
Bottom-left corner, with the y axis growing upward
quiz.explanation: Unlike UIKit, SpriteKit has y pointing up, with the scene's default 'anchorPoint' at (0, 0). Forgetting this produces upside-down or off-screen nodes.

quiz.question: When is the 'update(_:)' method called?
options: Every frame, before actions and physics are evaluated
Only once, when the scene is presented
Only when the user touches the screen
quiz.explanation: It is the heart of the game loop. 'currentTime' lets you compute the time between frames for frame-rate-independent movement.

quiz.question: What is the role of 'contactTestBitMask'?
options: It defines which bodies collide physically
It defines which categories the body generates contact notifications for
quiz.explanation: 'collisionBitMask' controls physical collision; 'contactTestBitMask' controls notifications sent to the 'contactDelegate'. By default, 'contactTestBitMask' is zero and no contact is reported.

quiz.question: What must you configure for 'didBegin(_:)' to be called?
quiz.explanation: The physics world's delegate receives the contact, and the body must declare which categories it wants to be told about. Without both, the method never fires.

quiz.question: Which approach is correct for creating the scene in SwiftUI?
options: Create a new scene on every evaluation of 'body'
Create the 'SKScene' once, in a property, and pass it to the 'SpriteView'
quiz.explanation: 'body' can be re-evaluated many times. Creating the scene in it may restart the game. Keep it in a stable property ('@State' or a constant).

quiz.question: How does GameKit identify the player in Game Center?
options: By asking for the player's email in a text field
By mandatorily creating an account of your own
quiz.explanation: The 'authenticateHandler' is called by the system, which shows the Game Center login screen if needed. Only after authentication can scores be submitted.

quiz.question: The game is slow and 'showsNodeCount' shows thousands of nodes. What is the best action?
options: Remove off-screen nodes and reuse textures with an atlas
quiz.explanation: Each node costs drawing and simulation time. Removing nodes that left the screen and grouping textures into atlases reduces draw calls.

quiz.question: What are achievements for in Game Center?
options: To store game progress in the cloud
To recognize player milestones, reported via 'GKAchievement'
quiz.explanation: Achievements are configured in App Store Connect and reported by the app when the player reaches the milestone. Leaderboards are for comparing scores.

extraQuiz.question: Which node displays text in SpriteKit?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'SKLabelNode' draws a string with configurable font and size. 'SKSpriteNode' is for images and solid colors.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'SKAction.sequence([a, b])' do?
options: It runs a and b at the same time
It runs actions a and b one after the other
It repeats a and b forever
extraQuiz.explanation: 'sequence' runs in order and 'group' in parallel. To repeat forever, wrap it in 'repeatForever'.

extraQuiz.question: Which property enables showing the frame rate during development?
extraQuiz.explanation: 'showsFPS' and 'showsNodeCount' help diagnose performance. They should be turned off in the release build.

extraQuiz.question: What does 'didMove(to:)' indicate?
options: The scene was presented in a view and is a good place to set up nodes
extraQuiz.explanation: It is called when the scene enters an 'SKView'. Many games create the scenery, the player and the 'contactDelegate' there.

extraQuiz.question: Why use 'SKTextureAtlas'?
options: To make the game work without images
To group textures and reduce loading and drawing costs
extraQuiz.explanation: Textures in an atlas can be loaded and drawn more efficiently, which improves performance and loading time.

extraQuiz.question: How do you submit a score to a Game Center leaderboard?
options: Authenticate the player and submit via 'GKLeaderboard' to the leaderboard ID
Save it in 'UserDefaults', which syncs automatically with Game Center
extraQuiz.explanation: The leaderboard is created in App Store Connect with an ID. The app submits the value through GameKit, after the player is authenticated.
